tasks.explain: The gap between sell-in and sell-out is a basic diagnostic metric in distribution. Shipments only mean the product left the manufacturer's warehouse; it becomes a sale only once an end buyer actually buys it. A steady ratio around one is a healthy picture. A sharp spike means the channel's stockpile is growing, and that's a deferred problem: the distributor will spend next quarter selling down inventory rather than ordering new stock. The opposite situation, a ratio noticeably below one, is also a signal; the channel is draining its stock and will soon hit a shortage.

tasks.title: Why the brand fell
tasks.brief: «Nettora» brand sales in Q1 2026 are half what they were in Q1 2024. Management wants an explanation. The decline has already been decomposed into components, and the picture across the first quarters is shown above the query in abridged form.
tasks.goal: Determine the cause of the decline from the decomposition results.
tasks.predictQuestion: What was the main cause of the drop in brand sales?

options.label: Loss of distribution: more than half the outlets stopped carrying the brand
options.why: The outlet count dropped from 79 to 37 (more than half), while sales per outlet barely changed: 127.9 vs. 116.4. Demand is alive wherever the brand is still on the shelf; what disappeared was shelf access itself.

options.label: A drop in demand: shoppers switched to other brands
options.why: A demand drop would first show up as lower sales per outlet. Here that figure stays within about ten percent, within normal fluctuation.

options.label: A price too high pushed buyers away
options.why: Price rose from 184.7 to 203.8 (about 10% over two years), which is below inflation and doesn't explain a halving. A price effect would also have shown up in sales per outlet.

options.label: Seasonality: Q1 is weak for household chemicals
options.why: Seasonality is ruled out by the design: matching quarters of different years are compared. That's exactly why decompositions are built year over year, not quarter over quarter.

hints: Break total units down into two factors: number of outlets and sales per outlet.
See which factor moved more.
tasks.explain: This is a standard analytical technique: any change is decomposed into factors, and the question reduces to which factor moved. Units = outlet count × sales per outlet; revenue = units × price; sales per outlet = purchase count × average basket. Once it's clear that distribution fell, not demand, the problem's owner changes too: this isn't a question for marketing or pricing, it's for the field team and chain negotiations. In FMCG this metric is measured formally as numeric distribution (share of outlets carrying the product) and weighted distribution (the same share, weighted by outlet turnover). A drop in weighted distribution alone means the brand fell out of specifically the large outlets, which is far worse.

tasks.title: Weeks of cover at a distributor
tasks.brief: The CFO is worried about write-offs: the «Setouchi Trading» distributor is showing large warehouse stock of the «Aqualis» brand. You need to work out how many weeks of sales it will cover at the current sales pace of the outlets it serves.
tasks.goal: Return one row: units_on_hand (stock of «Aqualis Still 0.5 L» at the «Setouchi Trading» distributor at the end of December 2025), avg_weekly_units (average weekly sales of this product at the outlets served by the distributor, October–December 2025, rounded to one decimal place) and weeks_cover (how many weeks the stock will last at that sales pace, rounded to one decimal place).
hints: Warehouse stock lives in a separate table, fact_stock, with no direct link to fact_sellout: pull the needed number with a separate scalar subquery, as in sql-014.
Compute the weekly sales pace only from this distributor's outlets; filter on c.served_by_distributor_id, not on all sales of the product nationwide.
tasks.explain: Weeks of cover is a standard way to see stock not in units, but in time: 1,315 units mean nothing on their own, but nearly 22 weeks of cover at the average sales pace signals serious overstocking, on FMCG products with limited shelf life, that's a direct write-off risk. A healthy level is usually 3–6 weeks depending on the category; anything noticeably higher means either an ordering mistake or a sharp slowdown in outlet sales that the warehouse hasn't reflected yet. This is the same diagnostic move as sell-in/sell-out in sql-022, just for stock instead of the shipment flow.

tasks.title: Who missed the plan in December
tasks.brief: In early January, the sales manager reconciles actuals against the December 2025 plan and asks for a list of reps who missed their revenue target within their division, only those under 100% attainment.
tasks.goal: For December 2025, return rep_name, target_revenue (rounded to whole numbers), actual_revenue (revenue from the rep's division products at the rep's outlets, rounded to whole numbers) and attainment_pct (the plan attainment percentage, rounded to one decimal place). Only role = 'rep' and attainment_pct < 100. Ordered by attainment_pct ascending.
hints: The plan is tied to a rep and a division at once. Join the fact to the plan on both keys, rep_id and division.
A LEFT JOIN is needed in case a rep had no sales at all in their division in December: then actual should become 0, not vanish from the report, COALESCE(a.revenue, 0), as in sql-014.
tasks.explain: The plan and the actuals sit at different granularities that aren't obvious at first glance: fact_target holds one row per rep and division per month, while fact_sellout is a scatter of sales across outlets and products, from which the rep's division still has to be assembled through two joins. LEFT JOIN is essential here for the same reason as in sql-014: a rep with zero sales in December shouldn't disappear from the report, on the contrary, that's precisely the most interesting case, 0% attainment. The filter attainment_pct < 100 belongs in WHERE, not HAVING, because the calculation runs over ordinary columns of the join result: the aggregates are already computed inside the actual CTE, and there's no grouping at this level of the query.

tasks.title: Why «Aqualis» revenue holds up even as volume falls
tasks.brief: The «Aqualis» brand's unit sales volume in Q1 2025 dropped noticeably compared to Q1 2024, but in the presentation revenue looks almost unscathed. The CFO wants the discrepancy explained. Above the query are «Aqualis» totals for the first quarters of both years.
tasks.goal: Determine the cause from the decomposition results.
tasks.predictQuestion: What happened to the «Aqualis» brand between Q1 2024 and Q1 2025?

options.label: Price was raised by almost 20%, which offset a nearly quarter-size drop in volume: revenue holds up on price, not demand
options.why: Units fell from 26,531 to 20,482 (−23%), while the average price rose from 53 to 63.4 (+20%); as a result revenue dipped only 7.6%, even though the real physical sales volume shrank much more sharply.

options.label: Demand grew, since revenue barely changed
options.why: Revenue is price times volume, and it can hold steady even under falling demand if price rises faster than volume falls. That's exactly what happened here.

options.label: The brand lost distribution, like «Nettora» in sql-023
options.why: Outlet count didn't change, 88 in both years. That's exactly the difference that separates this case from sql-023: there the cause was losing shelf space; here the shelf space is intact, and price is what changed.

options.label: The figures fell because of Q1 seasonality
options.why: Seasonality is ruled out by comparing the same quarter across different years, the same reasoning as in sql-023.

hints: Compare the rate of change in units against the rate of change in average price, which is larger in magnitude?
The outlet count is identical in both years; that immediately rules out one of the usual causes.
tasks.explain: Revenue is a deceptive front: it can barely move while two opposing shifts happen underneath it and cancel each other out. Here a 23% drop in physical volume is almost entirely masked by a 20% price increase; the resulting 7.6% revenue dip looks like "everything's fine", even though the real problem, lost sales volume, hasn't gone anywhere. The outlets figure is worth noting separately: it's identical in both years, which is exactly why the distribution-loss story (as in sql-023) doesn't apply here; there the cause was vanishing shelf space, here the shelf space is intact and it's the price and volume on it that changed. Practical takeaway: always break stable-looking revenue down into price and volume separately before concluding a brand is holding steady.

tasks.title: How many products make up half of revenue
tasks.brief: Ahead of an assortment review, a category manager wants to gauge portfolio concentration: if half the annual revenue comes from a handful of SKUs, dropping any one of them is a serious risk; if revenue is spread across the whole lineup, the risk is lower.
tasks.goal: For 2025, determine the smallest set of top-revenue products that together account for at least 50% of annual revenue. Return product_name, revenue (rounded to whole numbers) and cum_share_pct (the cumulative share of total revenue in percent, rounded to one decimal place). Ordered by revenue descending.
hints: Cumulative share is the same trick as the running total in sql-054, just with the result additionally divided by the grand total and converted to a percentage.
To include exactly the rows needed to reach 50%, compare the share accumulated BEFORE the current row (without it) against the threshold. If it was already under 50%, this row is needed.
tasks.explain: The idea is to include the minimal set of leaders in the report, not an arbitrary top N: what's compared isn't the current row's own cumulative share, but the share accumulated BEFORE it (prev_share_pct); that's what decides whether this row was necessary to cross 50%. The result: 15 out of 47 products, roughly a third of the lineup, together account for just over half of revenue, moderate, not extreme concentration; not the case of five hits carrying the whole company, but not a perfectly even spread either. It's easy to go wrong here by expecting the classic "20% of products drive 80% of revenue" rule: this portfolio doesn't bear it out, and forcing a conclusion to match someone else's heuristic instead of reading your own numbers is a typical interpretation mistake.

tasks.title: Eight customers, half the revenue
tasks.brief: The CFO is preparing for annual terms negotiations and asks how dependent the company is on individual customers: whose departure would really show up in the report, and whose would pass unnoticed.
tasks.goal: Measure revenue concentration by customer for 2025, then answer what those shares say about the company dependence.

steps.goal: For 2025, return the eight customers with the highest revenue: customer_name, chain_name, revenue (rounded to whole numbers) and share_pct, the customer share of 2025 revenue in percent, rounded to one decimal. Sorted by revenue descending.
hints: The denominator of the share is revenue from all customers over the same period, not the revenue of these eight: take it from a separate subquery on fact_sellout with the same date condition.
LIMIT is applied after sorting and after the share is computed, so trimming the output can be the last thing you do: it does not affect the denominator.

steps.question: The top row is 8.9% of annual revenue, the lowest of the eight is 4.3%. No single customer accounts for even a tenth. Does that mean the company has no dependence on any individual customer?
hints: Look at the chain_name column: how many distinct values are there, and how many rows fall on the most frequent one?

options.label: No: the eight rows are outlets of four chains, and the contract is signed with the chain. Three Bazario warehouses together account for almost a fifth of revenue.
options.why: The grain of a row here is a warehouse, the grain of the decision is a contract with a chain. Until the two are reconciled, the largest counterparty looks half its real size.

options.label: Yes: the maximum is 8.9%, that is low concentration, and the risk of a single customer can be treated as immaterial.
options.why: The number is right, the conclusion is not: the rows are independent only on paper. Three of the eight warehouses belong to one chain and leave with its contract, not one by one.

options.label: No: the shares are computed against the revenue of these eight, so they say nothing about the dependence of the company.
options.why: The denominator here is all 2025 revenue, not the revenue of the eight. The numbers themselves show it: the shares add up to half, not to a hundred percent.

options.label: Yes: all eight are warehouses of online platforms, and a warehouse is not a customer, so concentration should be measured by channel and the question about customers is meaningless.
options.why: Channel is a useful cut, but it answers a different question. Dependence is measured by whoever signed the contract, and such a counterparty does exist here: the chain.

tasks.explain: This task is about the gap between the grain of the data and the grain of the decision. In fact_sellout a customer is a delivery point, and row by row the concentration looks moderate: 8.9% at most. But negotiations happen with a chain, not with a warehouse, and three rows in the same table belong to Bazario, 18.6% together, twice the largest single customer. The move carries over almost word for word: SKU versus brand, sales rep versus team, distributor warehouse versus the distributor itself. Before naming a concentration figure, ask at what level the decision in question is made, then aggregate up to it.

tasks.title: Which region is really stronger
tasks.brief: The head of regional development is planning next year's budget and asks which regions actually sell better, not in absolute totals but adjusted for the size of the region itself.
tasks.goal: Work out revenue and revenue per capita for every region in 2025, then answer which region is really stronger: the one that leads by absolute revenue, or the one that leads by revenue per capita.

steps.goal: For 2025, return for every region: region_name, population (the region's population), revenue (total revenue, rounded to whole numbers), and revenue_per_capita (revenue divided by population, rounded to two decimals). Sorted by revenue descending.
hints: revenue is already in the starter query. revenue_per_capita is that same revenue from the same row, divided by r.population, not by the sum across all regions.
No extra JOIN is needed: r.population already comes from dim_region, which the query already joins.

steps.question: By revenue the top row is Saitama, with revenue_per_capita of 0.92. Miyagi, only third in the overall ranking, has revenue_per_capita of 2.46. Does Saitama's higher total revenue mean it is the stronger market by penetration?
hints: Schema: every region has its own population (dim_region.population), and it varies a lot in size. What does that mean for comparing raw revenue?

options.label: No: Saitama has the highest total revenue, but its revenue_per_capita is only 0.92, against 2.46 for Miyagi. Miyagi sells markedly more intensely per resident, even though it is only third by total revenue.
options.why: Total revenue grows with market size on its own: Saitama's population is 7,340,000, Miyagi's is 2,260,000, more than three times smaller. Dividing revenue by population shows Saitama beats Miyagi in total mainly because its market is bigger, not because brands sell more intensely there per resident.

options.label: Yes: the highest total revenue is direct proof that Saitama is the strongest market by penetration.
options.why: The number is right, the conclusion is not: the total grows with market size on its own. Saitama's population is nearly three times Miyagi's (7,340,000 versus 2,260,000), so a higher total revenue is expected regardless of how intensely each resident buys.

options.label: No, but revenue_per_capita is beside the point: it is the region's share of total revenue across all regions, not a division by its population, so it cannot be used to compare regions.
options.why: That is not so: revenue_per_capita here is this region's revenue divided by this region's population, the same row. It exists precisely to compare regions of different sizes, not to show a share of total revenue.

options.label: The question does not make sense: distribution decisions are made at the level of individual outlets, not whole regions, so comparing regions is pointless.
options.why: Decisions about specific outlets are indeed made further down, but before deciding where to focus effort you need to know which regions are underusing their potential in the first place, and that is a regional-level question, not one that reduces to a single outlet.

tasks.explain: This task is about totals not measuring intensity when the groups being compared are different sizes. Saitama leads in revenue simply because its market is bigger: population 7,340,000 against 2,260,000 for Miyagi. Once revenue is divided by the size of the base (revenue_per_capita), the picture changes: Miyagi sells almost three times more intensely per resident, even though it trails Saitama and Aichi in absolute terms. The move carries over to any pair of "total plus group size": revenue per outlet instead of total chain revenue, average receipt per customer instead of total sales, conversion instead of visit count. Before comparing totals across groups of different sizes, ask how big those groups actually are.

tasks.title: Simple average price versus weighted
tasks.brief: A category manager got Aqualis's average price from the BI system and again from an analyst; the numbers differ by almost eight percent, and it is unclear which one belongs in the pricing report.
tasks.goal: Work out the simple and the volume-weighted average price for every brand in 2025, then answer which of the two numbers shows the price a customer actually pays per unit on average.

steps.goal: For 2025, return for every brand: brand, naive_avg_price (the simple average of avg_price values across all sales rows, rounded to two decimals), and weighted_avg_price (total revenue divided by total units, rounded to two decimals).
hints: naive_avg_price is already in the starter query, it is AVG(f.avg_price) across all rows. weighted_avg_price is not the average of another column; it is SUM(f.revenue) divided by SUM(f.units).
Round the same way as naive_avg_price: to two decimals.

steps.question: For Aqualis, naive_avg_price is 64.08, weighted_avg_price is 59.58: two numbers with the same name, "average price", that differ by almost eight percent. Can either one be used in the pricing report?
hints: Schema: the Aqualis brand has several SKUs (dim_product) at different prices and different sales volumes. How does that affect each of the two ways of averaging?

options.label: No: naive_avg_price averages price across sales rows, not across units sold, giving every SKU the same weight regardless of volume. The price a customer actually pays on average is weighted_avg_price, it is weighted by actual sales.
options.why: Aqualis has several SKUs at different prices and different sales volumes. naive_avg_price averages their prices equally, as if every SKU sold just as often. weighted_avg_price divides revenue by units and so accounts for each SKU's real weight in actual sales.

options.label: Yes: since both numbers are called "average price", either works for the report. The gap is under ten percent and will not change the overall conclusion.
options.why: Eight percent on price in a pricing report is a real difference, not noise. For some brands the weighted average even comes out higher than the simple one, not lower, so the direction of the gap is not consistent and cannot be written off as rounding.

options.label: No, but it is not about weighting: naive_avg_price is wrong because it only averages one randomly chosen week, not the whole of 2025.
options.why: That is not the case: AVG(f.avg_price) in this query runs over every week of 2025 with no exceptions, the same rows as SUM(f.revenue) and SUM(f.units). The gap is not about the period; it is about what gets averaged, prices row by row, or money and units summed first.

options.label: The question does not make sense: a brand with several SKUs at different prices has no single "true" average price at all, so there is nothing to compare.
options.why: A brand with several SKUs indeed has no single "correct" price on its own, but the question was not about that; it was about which of the two already-computed numbers is a usable estimate of it. weighted_avg_price qualifies, naive_avg_price does not: it is distorted by ignoring volume.

tasks.explain: This task is about "average" not being one number when the units being averaged are of different sizes. naive_avg_price is the arithmetic mean across sales rows: every week of every SKU weighs the same, no matter how many units it represents. weighted_avg_price is revenue divided by units: it weighs each row by how much was actually bought. Aqualis has several SKUs priced from 38 to 128 per unit with different sales volumes, so the simple average and the true average purchase price diverge by almost eight percent. The move carries over to any pair of "simple average of a metric" and "sum of the numerator divided by sum of the denominator": average receipt, average margin, average rating. If the weights differ, the two numbers are bound to diverge, and the question is always the same: what is weighted, and what is not.

tasks.title: A week with a promotion and a week without one
tasks.brief: Trade marketing and sales are arguing: one side says the «Milvara» promotions work, the other says the brand is growing anyway. The argument comes down to two numbers nobody has: how much the brand sells in a week with a promotion and in a week without one.
tasks.goal: For 2025 and the brand «Milvara», return promo_week_units (average unit sales in a week that had a promotion) and base_week_units (the same for a week without one). Round both to whole numbers.
hints: A week counts as a promo week if it holds at least one row with promo_id filled in. That «at least one» is what MAX over a conditional 1 gives you.
AVG(CASE WHEN condition THEN units END) with no ELSE averages only the matching weeks: where CASE returns NULL, the row stays out of the average.
tasks.explain: This is the step without which no conversation about promotions can start: sales are rolled up to the week, and every week now carries a flag saying whether a promotion ran in it. In the fact table that flag lives at row level (one outlet, one SKU, one week), but the comparison happens between whole weeks, so CASE is lifted one level up by MAX: the week is a promo week if a promotion ran anywhere in it. Then AVG(CASE ... THEN units END) with no ELSE produces both averages in a single pass: NULL never enters an average, so promo weeks do not dilute the base and the base does not dilute the promo. «Milvara» came out at 2088 units in a promo week against 1337 without one, and that is already a conversation with numbers in it.

tasks.title: Lift for every brand
tasks.brief: The marketing director is splitting next year's promo budget across brands and wants one table: how much more a week with a promotion sells than an ordinary week, for every FMCG brand.
tasks.goal: For 2025 and every brand in the FMCG division, return brand, promo_week_units, base_week_units (both rounded to whole numbers) and lift_pct (how much higher the promo week is than the base week, in percent, rounded to one decimal). Sorted by lift_pct descending.
hints: The first step is already written: every week of every brand has its units and its promo flag. What remains is rolling weeks up into brands with GROUP BY brand.
Percentages: 100.0 * (promo - base) / base. The literal with a decimal point is mandatory, otherwise integer division throws the fraction away.
tasks.explain: Lift is a ratio, which is why it compares brands that sell in completely different volumes: «Aqualis» does 4875 units in a promo week and «Nettora» does 1041, yet +138.8% against +82.4% is a fair comparison. The analyst's work starts after that. «Nettora» sits second on lift and that says almost nothing about the health of the brand: the lift is measured against a base from the same year, and the base itself has fallen threefold in two years. Lift answers exactly one question, how different a week with a promotion is from a week without one in the same period, and it answers neither «is the brand growing» nor «did the promotion pay for itself». The second question needs money rather than units: that is sql-068 and sql-070.

tasks.title: One promotion, two bases
tasks.brief: The brand «Nettora» ran a 30% discount from 29 January to 17 February 2026. The category manager asks what it delivered. The query works out average weekly units for the brand three ways: across the promo weeks, across the four weeks before it, and across every week without a promotion in the whole history of the data.
tasks.goal: Work out which of the two comparisons answers the question «what did the promotion deliver».
tasks.predictQuestion: Against the four weeks before it, the promo week is 12.5% higher; against the average week without promotions across the whole history, it is 39.3% lower. What did the promotion deliver?

options.label: About +12% against the level the brand was at just before the promotion. The second figure measures the two-year decline of the brand itself, not the promotion.
options.why: The base «every week without a promotion» is mostly 2024, when «Nettora» still held shelf space in outlets it later lost. Comparing against it mixes two different changes: the effect of the promotion and a two-year decline. Only a base close in time separates them, which is where the four weeks before the start and the +12.5% come from.

options.label: The promotion failed: sales during it are 39% below an ordinary week for the brand.
options.why: An «ordinary week» here is an average over two and a half years, and the brand sold twice as much at the start of that period as at the end. Against such a base every week of 2026 looks like a failure, promotion or not, which means the base is not measuring the promotion.

options.label: The effect of the promotion is the gap between the two estimates: 51.8 percentage points.
options.why: The difference between two lifts measured against different bases is neither a lift nor an effect: it is the distance between two reference points, so it describes the bases rather than the promotion.

options.label: The numbers are not comparable: during the promotion the brand sold at a reduced price, so the comparison should use revenue rather than units.
options.why: Price would indeed interfere with a revenue comparison, which is exactly why volume lift is measured in units, where the discount has no direct effect. The revenue question is a fair one, but it is the next step (sql-068), not a reason to call these numbers incomparable.

hints: Look at which years the third base is made of: it holds three times more promotion-free weeks from 2024 to 2026 than from 2026 alone.
Ask yourself what happens to each of the two estimates if the brand has simply been declining slowly for two years.
tasks.explain: The base is a decision made by the analyst rather than a property of the data, and here it flips even the sign of the answer: +12.5% against -39.3% for one and the same promotion. Both figures are arithmetically correct, but they answer different questions. The four weeks before the start answer «what changed because of the promotion»: a brand does not change much by itself in a month, so the difference sits closest to the effect. The average week across the whole history answers «how is the brand doing compared with itself two years ago», which is a question about the decline of «Nettora», and the answer to it is correct; it simply is not about the promotion. Hence a rule of writing rather than of querying: the base is always named next to the lift. «Plus 12% against the four weeks before the start» is a number that can be checked and challenged; «plus 12%» is a number that means nothing.

tasks.title: The promotion ran in one channel only
tasks.brief: The promotion «Milvara: 2+1» ran from 5 to 20 May 2025 in modern trade only, but its lift was worked out across all sales of the brand, and it came out modest. The channel manager disagrees and asks for a recount inside his own channel. The base is the four weeks before the start, 7 April to 4 May: the brand had no promotions in them.
tasks.goal: Return two numbers: lift_all_pct (lift across all channels) and lift_modern_trade_pct (lift inside the modern_trade channel alone). Both in percent against the base weeks, rounded to one decimal.
hints: The periods are split by the start date of the promotion: weeks from 2025-05-05 onwards belong to the promotion, earlier weeks to the base.
Both columns use the same lift formula; only the measure changes, all_units against mt_units.
tasks.explain: Lift across all channels is 56.6%, lift inside the channel that ran the promotion is 207.2%: a gap of more than three times, and the smaller number here is not a cautious estimate, it is a wrong one. Both the numerator and the denominator of the first figure carry traditional retail, pharmacies and ecom, where no promotion ran at all: their sales dilute the effect the way water dilutes paint. The rule is simple and carries over to any promotion: the slice you measure lift on has to match the reach of the promotion. Channel is the most common mistake but not the only one. If a promotion ran in one chain, in one region, or on three SKUs out of six, the base and the period are cut the same way. The reach is right there in the reference table: every promotion in dim_promo has a channel column, and the value all is far from universal in it.

tasks.title: How much discount was given away
tasks.brief: Finance is putting together a promo budget review and wants one figure for the August promotion «Milvara: Discount 30%» (promo_id = 47): how much money was handed to the buyer as discount. Discount given is the difference between what the volume sold would have cost at list price and what was actually paid for it. The August price list sits in fact_price with month_start = 2025-08-01.
tasks.goal: For promo_id = 47, return units (units sold), promo_revenue (actual revenue), revenue_at_list (the same volume valued at list price) and discount_given (the discount handed over). Round every amount to whole numbers.
hints: Value at list price is worked out row by row and only then summed: SUM(f.units * pr.list_price), not the product of two sums.
Discount given is the difference between the two amounts you already have; it needs no third source.
tasks.explain: The promotion cost 231,546 yen of discount against 540,472 yen of revenue, which is 30.0% of the volume valued at list price. Matching the promised 30% is not a tautology but an execution check: retail chains stand between the promo calendar and the shelf, and actual discount depth drifts from plan in both directions. A query like this is the cheapest way to see that, and it is worth running across every promotion rather than only the suspicious ones. The figure then meets the other half of the question: discount given is what the promotion cost, and only a comparison against a base shows what it bought. The answer there is not the obvious one: sql-070.

tasks.title: Efficient on paper
tasks.brief: A finance analyst has sent over a summary of 2025 promotions that ran in every channel: how much discount was given away, how much revenue they brought in above the base of the four weeks before the start, and the ratio of the second to the first. He proposes a conclusion: shallow discounts are more efficient than deep ones, so from now on we only run those.
tasks.goal: Judge whether the proposed conclusion follows from this table.
tasks.predictQuestion: Does it follow from this table that shallow discounts are more efficient than deep ones?

options.label: No: the return falls with depth almost mechanically, because the denominator grows while the uplift here does not grow with depth at all. A conclusion about depth needs a like-for-like comparison, and this table has none.
options.why: Discount given grows with depth by definition: the same units, a bigger cut on each. The uplift in revenue, meanwhile, shows no relation to depth here (552 thousand for a ten percent promotion, 284 thousand for a thirty percent one), so the ratio falls almost arithmetically. And the table cannot tell apart the reasons the uplift failed to grow: different brands, different seasons, different durations, other brands running promotions at the same time.

options.label: Yes: a return of 4.8 against 0.7 is nearly a sevenfold gap, and a gap that size cannot be chance.
options.why: The size of a gap says nothing about its cause. The denominator for deep promotions is three times bigger by construction, and that alone produces a gap of several times even if the promotions work identically.

options.label: Yes, with one caveat: first check that all the promotions ran for the same length of time.
options.why: Duration does need to be levelled, but it is only one of the differences. There are different brands with different trajectories here, different seasons, and overlapping promotions: in 45 of the 122 promo weeks, three or more brands ran promotions at once.

options.label: The conclusion is wrong because the return is calculated wrongly: the denominator should be promo revenue rather than discount given.
options.why: Uplift over money spent is the usual way to measure promo payback: the denominator holds what was spent. The flaw in this table is not the formula but the fact that it compares promotions that are not comparable.

hints: Look at the two columns separately: how the denominator moves with depth, and how the numerator moves.
Ask what else, besides discount depth, differs between the rows of the table.
tasks.explain: Uplift over money spent is the right metric and a ready-made trap at the same time: it falls as the denominator grows, even when the numerator behaves identically. Here that is visible in pure form: the discount triples, the uplift does not grow, the return falls by roughly the same factor. The table does not show that shallow discounts are better; it shows that at this depth and this uplift the return is higher, and in this data the uplift has no relation to depth. A conclusion about depth needs promotions comparable in everything else: one brand, a similar season, the same duration, no other promotions running alongside. In practice this is achieved by design rather than by picking rows from history: the same mechanic runs in different chains at different depths and those are compared with each other. And even there the conclusion stays about revenue rather than profit: margin is not in this data at all, and a return of about 1.0 in revenue means a loss in money.

tasks.title: Was the promotion worth the discount
tasks.brief: The August promotion «Milvara: Discount 30%» looks like a success: unit sales grew almost two and a half times. sql-068 has already established that 231,546 yen of discount was given away on it. The sales director asks a different question: did the promotion bring in more money than it cost. The base is the four weeks before the start, 7 to 28 July.
tasks.goal: Work out the revenue of the three promo weeks, the same three weeks at base level, and the uplift between them, then say whether the promotion paid for the discount given.

steps.goal: For the brand «Milvara», return promo_revenue (revenue of the three promo weeks, 4 to 18 August), base_revenue (average weekly revenue of the four weeks from 7 to 28 July, multiplied by three) and incremental_revenue (the difference between them). Round all three to whole numbers.
hints: Promo revenue is the sum of three weeks; the base level is the average of four weeks multiplied by three. Summing the July weeks outright will not do: there are four of them, not three.
The uplift is the difference between those same two expressions; it needs no separate query.

steps.question: The three promo weeks delivered 540,472 yen of revenue against a base level of 313,934 yen, an uplift of 226,538 yen. You already worked out the discount given on this promotion in the previous task. What do you tell the sales director?
hints: Compare the two amounts head on: which is larger, the revenue uplift or the discount given?
Remember that revenue is not profit: the cost of the goods sold still has to come out of it.

options.label: Volume grew, but in money the promotion did not pay for itself: the revenue uplift of 226,538 yen is smaller than the 231,546 yen given away as discount, and in profit the gap is wider still, because uplift brings the company only its margin while the discount is lost in full.
options.why: The growth in units was real (3327 against 1353 per week), but every unit went out 30% cheaper, so in money the uplift did not even reach the discount given: 226,538 against 231,546 yen. And that is the optimistic reading: revenue uplift yields the company only its margin share, while the discount is gone entirely.

options.label: The promotion paid for itself: revenue of the three promo weeks, 540,472 yen, is much larger than the 231,546 yen of discount given.
options.why: That compares the wrong pair. Promo revenue includes what the brand would have sold anyway, the base level of 313,934 yen. Payback is measured only by the uplift over that base, and the uplift is 226,538 yen, which is less than the discount given.

options.label: The promotion worked: volume grew two and a half times, and that is what promotions are for.
options.why: Volume growth is a result of the promotion but not an answer about payback: the volume was bought with a discount, and the question is precisely whether it was worth the money. Here the revenue uplift did not cover the discount given.

options.label: The question cannot be answered: without the cost of goods, promo payback cannot be calculated at all.
options.why: Cost of goods is indeed missing for a precise profit answer, but it is not needed to see the main point: the revenue uplift of 226,538 yen is already smaller than the 231,546 yen of discount, and margin can only widen that gap. Missing data prevents refining the conclusion, not reaching it.

tasks.explain: This is the whole review in one task: a promotion with an obvious success in units turned out to be a loss in money, and the entire difference lies in what it is compared against. A revenue uplift of 226,538 yen against 231,546 yen of discount given means every yen of discount came back as a yen of revenue and not one yen more, and revenue is not profit. Three things are worth taking away. First: payback is measured by uplift over a base, never by promo revenue, otherwise every promotion pays for itself, since the brand would have sold anyway. Second: growth in units and growth in money diverge the deeper the discount goes, and the first without the second is not an argument. Third: even a return of about one in revenue is a loss in profit rather than a break-even. What this review cannot work out is the true cost of the promotion: neither cost of goods nor display and print costs are in the data, so the answer here is an upper bound on payback, and it should be spoken as exactly that.

tasks.title: What reached the till
tasks.brief: The «Aqualis» brand manager is preparing a price list revision and asks how much the company actually receives per unit. The price list says one thing, the till says another: promotions and retailer discounts sit in between. The price list is stored by month in fact_price.
tasks.goal: For 2025 and the brand «Aqualis», return realized_price (actual revenue per unit sold), list_price (the same unit at list) and realization_pct (what percentage of the list price reached the till). Round all three to one decimal.
hints: The actual price per unit is all revenue divided by all units, not the average of the avg_price column: rows carry different volumes and cannot weigh the same.
Realization is the ratio of two sums you already have: actual revenue over that same revenue at list price.
tasks.explain: The price list is what the company intends, the till is what happened, and the gap between them has a price of its own: for «Aqualis» 91.7% of the list price reached the till, that is 59.6 yen out of 65.0. It can only be measured weighted: revenue divided by units, never averaged across rows. The reason is that fact rows come in different sizes, and a hundred units in a hypermarket and three units in a kiosk weigh the same in a plain average and nothing alike in money. The same rule holds wherever the word «average» appears: average price, average discount and average basket are all sums divided by sums, while AVG across rows answers a question nobody asked.

tasks.title: Who gives away the most
tasks.brief: The commercial director wants one page before the budget committee: for every brand, how much of the list price reaches the till and how many units sell on promotion. He wants to see whether the two columns are related.
tasks.goal: For 2025 and every brand, return brand, realization_pct (the percentage of the list price that reached the till) and promo_share_units (the share of promotion in units sold). Round both to one decimal. Sorted by realization_pct ascending.
hints: Promo share in units is a conditional sum over the full one: SUM(CASE WHEN promo_id IS NOT NULL THEN units ELSE 0 END) over SUM(units).
Both shares are worked out in a single pass over the same rows; no second query is needed.
tasks.explain: The two columns run almost as mirror images: «Rhinolar» sells 55.1% of its units on promotion and brings 86.7% of the list price to the till, while «Nettora» sells 23.4% and brings 96.1%. That is the main lever of price realization: the more volume goes through promotions, the lower the average price received, even if the list price never moved. But the mirror is imperfect, and that is the other half of the answer: «Aqualis» with a 35.5% promo share gives away more than «Vitanor» at 46.4%, because the «Aqualis» promotions are deeper. There are two levers, share of volume on promotion and depth of discount, and a conversation about price without both turns into an argument about who is to blame. The third lever, the mix of SKUs sold, waits in sql-074.

tasks.title: Two shares of one promotion
tasks.brief: In the meeting someone says «our promo share is 55%», the finance deck says 48%, and both numbers describe the same brand in the same year. Nobody is wrong: one was measured in units, the other in money. The director asks to see both side by side for every brand.
tasks.goal: For 2025 and every brand, return brand, promo_share_units (the share of promotion in units sold) and promo_share_revenue (the share of promotion in revenue). Round both to one decimal. Sorted by promo_share_units descending.
hints: Both shares are built the same way: a conditional sum divided by the full one. Only the measure changes, units in the first and revenue in the second.
Each share keeps its own denominator: units over units, money over money.
tasks.explain: The promo share in units is always higher than the share in money, and that is arithmetic rather than a data mismatch: a promo unit sold cheaper, so it weighs less in a money denominator. «Rhinolar» shows 55.1% against 48.3%, «Milvara» 17.7% against 13.0%, and the gap widens the deeper the discount. The practical conclusion is not about SQL: the question «what is our promo share» has no single answer, and the first move is to pin down the unit of measure. Units answer «how much product leaves on promotion», which is a conversation about shelf and production; money answers «how much revenue comes from promotion», which is a conversation about the P&L. Quoted without a unit, 55% and 48% look like somebody made a mistake, and the meeting goes on hunting for the culprit instead of deciding anything.

tasks.title: A discount nobody promised
tasks.brief: The «Aqualis» brand ran four promotions in 2025: one yellow tag at 12% and three at 30% off. An analyst worked out the actual discount across all promo sales of the brand for the year and got 23.4%, a number that appears nowhere in the promo calendar. Finance wants to know where it came from.
tasks.goal: Work out where an average discount that matches none of the promised ones comes from.
tasks.scenario:
Promotion          Discount   Units
Discount 30% (x3)        30   30325
Yellow tag               12   17482

Actual, total          23.4   47807
tasks.predictQuestion: Why is the actual discount for the brand over the year 23.4%, when the promises were 12% and 30%?

options.label: It is a volume-weighted average: 30% applied to 30,325 units and 12% to 17,482, and the weight of each depth sets the result.
options.why: It checks out on paper: (30 x 30325 + 12 x 17482) / 47807 = 23.4. The number has to land between 12 and 30, and closer to 30, because nearly two thirds of the volume went through the deep promotions. It cannot appear anywhere in the calendar: the calendar states mechanics, while the fact is made of how much sold under each of them.

options.label: The shelf discounts did not match what was promised: the retailers gave a different depth than agreed.
options.why: That is always worth checking, but not the case here: taken promotion by promotion, the actual discount matches the promised one to within a tenth (30.0, 12.0, 30.0, 30.1). Only the yearly total diverges, and it diverges by composition rather than by execution.

options.label: It is the plain average of the promised depths: (12 + 30) / 2 = 21, adjusted for sales outside promotions.
options.why: A plain average of two depths gives 21, not 23.4, and it means nothing anyway: averaging percentages without weighting by volume is the same mistake as averaging prices without weighting by units. Sales outside promotions do not enter this calculation at all; it covers promo sales only.

options.label: Distributor discounts from fact_sellin leaked into the figure, which is why it does not match the promo calendar.
options.why: The calculation runs on fact_sellout, that is sales in outlets, and distributor discounts are not part of it. Mixing sell-in and sell-out is a real mistake, but it cannot explain this particular number.

hints: Try to produce 23.4 from the four numbers in the table: two depths and two volumes.
Ask yourself where the result lands if the deep promotion sold twice as much as the shallow one.
tasks.explain: This is the third lever of price after depth and promo share: the mix, not «what discount» but «how much sold under each». A weighted average discount is under no obligation to match any promised one, and demanding that match is a classic checking mistake. Two practical consequences follow. First: plan and actual can only be compared at one level, promotion against promotion, never a yearly total against a calendar. Second: the yearly total moves even when every promotion ran exactly as promised, since it is enough for volume to shift from a shallow mechanic to a deep one. Which is why «the actual discount went from 20% to 23%» accuses nobody by itself: the first thing to look at is whether the mix changed.

tasks.title: The month the price sank furthest
tasks.brief: Finance sees a flat list price for «Aqualis» all year and revenue per unit jumping about. They want the monthly picture: where exactly the price sank, and whether that matches the promotions.
tasks.goal: For 2025 and the brand «Aqualis», return month in YYYY-MM format, realized_price (revenue per unit that month) and promo_share_units (the share of promotion in that month's units). Round both numbers to one decimal. Sorted by month ascending.
hints: The month comes out of the week date with the same five characters as in sql-010: substr(week_start, 1, 7).
Group by the same expression as the first column; you need not repeat it, the column number is enough.
tasks.explain: The monthly picture answers a question the yearly total hides. The lowest price for «Aqualis» is not in April, when all 100% of units went on promotion at 57.2 yen, but in June: 53.2 yen at a promo share of 60.8%. The explanation is not in the share but in the depth: the April yellow tag gave 12%, the June promotion 30%. The two levers work independently, and neither one is visible in a single column. Hence a working habit: monthly price realization with promo share beside it is the cheapest chart there is in a pricing negotiation, because it answers «we raised the price, why did the money not follow» on sight. And the third month worth noting is February, with no promotion at all and a price matching the list: that is the check that the calculation itself is sound.

tasks.title: The price list went up and the money went down
tasks.brief: The «Milvara» list price was raised in early 2026, and the commercial director expects revenue per unit to grow. Finance says they are receiving less than a year ago. We compare the first half of 2026 with the first half of 2025 and find out who is right.
tasks.goal: Work out the list price, the actual price per unit and the promo share for the first halves of 2025 and 2026, then explain why the price increase never reached the till.

steps.goal: For the brand «Milvara» across the first half of 2025 and the first half of 2026, return year, list_price (list price per unit sold), realized_price (actual revenue per unit) and promo_share_units (the share of promotion in units). Round all three to one decimal. Sorted by year ascending.
hints: The year comes out of the week date as its first four characters: substr(week_start, 1, 4).
The list price per unit sold is weighted by volume: SUM(units * list_price) / SUM(units), otherwise expensive SKUs weigh as much as the fast-moving ones.

steps.question: The list price per unit sold rose from 76.8 to 77.7 yen, while the price actually received fell from 74.3 to 70.4 yen. The promo share in units moved from 9.9% to 31.7% over the same period. What do you tell the commercial director?
hints: Look at the percentage change in each of the three figures.
Ask which of them is a decision the company made and which is a consequence of how it sold.

options.label: The list price did go up, but the share of volume sold on promotion tripled and took the increase away with room to spare: 90.6% of the list price reaches the till against 96.7% a year earlier.
options.why: The list price rose 1.2% while the price received fell 5.2%, and the gap is explained entirely by the third column: promo volume went from 9.9% to 31.7%. The pricing decision was carried out; the promo plan overrode it. Those are different decisions made by different people, and a conversation about price without the second column always ends in an argument about whose data is right.

options.label: The data contradicts itself: if the list price went up, the price received cannot fall, so the calculation is wrong somewhere.
options.why: There is no contradiction. The list price is the price before discounts, the received price is after them, and the promo share stands in between. It tripled, which is more than enough to swallow the increase and pull the price down.

options.label: The brand moved into cheaper outlets, so the average price fell.
options.why: A plausible and checkable theory, but not needed here: the gap is already explained by the promo share, which tripled. A channel shift would explain a fall without any promotion, and here there is a direct cause in the same data.

options.label: The increase came too late: it simply had no time to show up in first-half revenue.
options.why: The list price per unit sold is already worked out from the actual sales of both halves, so the increase is in the figure: 77.7 against 76.8. There is no lag here, there is a discount on top of the new list price.

tasks.explain: The review the whole skill exists for: «we raised the price» and «we receive less» are both true at once, and there is nothing to argue about once three numbers sit side by side. The list price rose 1.2%, the received price fell 5.2%, the promo share went from 9.9% to 31.7%, and price realization sank from 96.7% to 90.6%. Pricing is owned by the commercial function, the promo plan by trade marketing, and without a shared table each of them is sure they did their job. Hence a reporting rule: price is never shown as a single line. Three at a minimum, list, actual and promo share; four is better, with discount depth added. What this data will not show is how much the company earned on any of it. There is no cost of goods in it, so the conversation stays about revenue per unit rather than margin, and it should be spoken that way.

tasks.title: How far off we are
tasks.brief: The supply chain director is putting together the annual review and asks for a single number: how far the demand forecast sits from actual sales. The planner has no such number, only a feeling that «on the whole it is fine». Forecasts are stored as snapshots in fact_forecast_snapshot: a row is made in advance and never rewritten afterwards, and lag_months says how many months before the month started it was made.
tasks.goal: For 2025 and forecasts made one month ahead, return wmape_pct: the sum of misses without their sign as a percentage of the sum of actuals. Round to one decimal.
hints: Actuals are stored by week and the forecast by month, so it is the actuals that need rolling up: the first step already does it and gives the same «month and SKU» grain the forecast was made at.
The sign is removed before the adding: SUM(ABS(...)), not ABS(SUM(...)). The second way lets a shortfall in one month cancel an overshoot in another, and the error slides towards zero.
tasks.explain: The first number that makes any conversation about the forecast possible: in 2025 the one month ahead forecast missed by 15.3% of actuals. It is a sum divided by a sum, and each sum earns its place. The ABS in the numerator stops the misses from cancelling: a month short and a month over are two errors rather than none, and somebody paid for both, in idle lines or in write-offs. The denominator makes the number comparable: 15.3% reads the same for a brand selling three hundred thousand units and for one selling twenty thousand. The horizon here is the easiest one, a month ahead, when almost everything is already known. Next to the other horizons this figure will look far better than it is.

tasks.title: The further the horizon, the worse it gets
tasks.brief: Production plans line loading three months ahead and asks whether the far month can be trusted as much as the near one. The snapshots hold all three horizons: the same month forecast one, two and three months before it started.
tasks.goal: Across all months in the table return lag_months, pairs (how many «month and SKU» pairs are compared at each horizon) and wmape_pct, the error as a percentage of actuals, rounded to one decimal. Sorted by lag_months ascending.
hints: The horizon is already written into the snapshot row, so group by it and derive nothing from the dates.
The pair count belongs next to the error for a reason: the horizons hold different numbers of pairs, and without that column there is no telling whether the three figures are comparable.
tasks.explain: Error grows with the horizon: 15.4% one month ahead, 27% at two months and 30.9% at three. That is a property of time rather than of the model. A month before the start you already know the retailer orders, the promo plan and the stock in the channel; three months out you know none of it. The figures then read like this: the promise «we plan a quarter ahead» rests on a number twice as bad as the one usually cited in its defence. The pairs column is not decoration either. The far horizon holds fewer pairs, 1252 against 1344, because the earliest months of history have no snapshot made that far in advance, and three errors can only be compared knowing the sets almost coincide.

tasks.title: The tail that spoils the average
tasks.brief: In the planner report the error is worked out for every «month and SKU» pair and then averaged across rows. At the three month horizon that gives 35.6%, and nobody wants to walk into the committee with such a figure. Before arguing about it, work out who creates it.
tasks.goal: At the three month horizon, split the pairs into small (actuals below 200 units) and large ones and return size_group ('small' or 'large'), pairs, mape_pct (the error averaged across rows, in percent), wmape_pct (the same error weighted) and abs_error_units (the sum of misses in units). Round the percentages to one decimal.
hints: The starter already pairs forecast with actuals. One flag column is missing: a CASE on the actuals splits the pairs into two groups, and the grouping runs on that same column.
The two metrics differ only in where the division happens. The row average is an AVG of a percentage worked out inside each row; the weighted one is the sum of misses divided by the sum of actuals.
tasks.explain: The difference between two ways of counting the same thing turned out to sit entirely in the tail: pairs below two hundred units are 331 rows out of 1252, their row averaged error is 49.2% against 30.7% for the large ones, and in units they contribute 15 894 misses out of 302 935, which is 5.2%. That is where the 35.6% in the report comes from: across rows a SKU selling forty units weighs as much as one selling ten thousand, and the tail pulls the figure up. The weighted error answers «how many units did we get wrong», the row average answers «how predictable is a typical SKU». The second question is a fair one, but it is a different one: it decides which items to plan by hand, not how much raw material to order. Showing one metric in place of the other means answering a question nobody asked.

tasks.title: Which number goes to the committee
tasks.brief: The planner is preparing the regular slide and asks which single error metric to use. Both are worked out on exactly the same «month and SKU» pairs at the three month horizon, and they differ only in where the division sits.
tasks.goal: Predict what the query returns and explain the gap between the two numbers.
tasks.predictQuestion: Which numbers will the query return, and why did they come apart?

options.label: Around 35.6 and 30.9: across rows a small pair weighs as much as a large one, and the tail of small SKUs pulls the first number up
options.why: AVG divides by the number of rows, so a pair of forty units affects the result as much as a pair of ten thousand. Small pairs carry a high percentage by their nature: a miss of twenty units on a base of forty is 50%, and almost nothing in units. The weighted metric divides a sum by a sum, and the weight goes back to volume.

options.label: The two numbers will match: this is one metric written in two ways, differing only in the order of operations
options.why: The order of operations is the metric here. An average of ratios and a ratio of sums agree exactly when every row is the same size, and in the fact table they differ by a factor of hundreds.

options.label: The weighted one will come out higher: large SKUs weigh more in it, and that is where the error in units sits
options.why: In units the error really does sit almost entirely on large SKUs, but the weighted metric divides it by an equally large volume of actuals. The higher figure is the one where small pairs get an unearned weight, which is the row average.

options.label: Around 35.6 and 30.9, and the gap means some pairs have zero actuals, where the percentage error runs to infinity
options.why: The numbers are right and the reason is not. Pairs with zero actuals never enter the comparison at all: actuals arrive through the join, so a month without sales is simply absent. The gap is created by equal weight on rows of unequal size, not by a division by zero.

hints: Look at what sits inside AVG in the first column and at what is divided by what in the second.
Picture two pairs: forty units of actuals with a miss of twenty, and ten thousand units with a miss of a thousand. Work out both metrics on them by hand.
tasks.explain: Two metrics, the same data, and almost five points between them: 35.6% against 30.9%. The only difference is the weight of a row. The row average treats every «month and SKU» pair as equal, so the tail of small items, where a miss of twenty units reads as 50%, lifts the total. The weighted one counts units, and in it the same tail holds 5.2% of the error. What goes to the supply chain committee is the weighted figure: the decisions there are how much raw material to order and how many shifts to run, and those are questions about units. The row average stays inside planning as a way to find items that cannot be predicted at all, and there it beats the weighted one. The metric follows the decision, not the number that looks nicer.

tasks.title: The brand we always overshoot
tasks.brief: At the accuracy review the commercial director says the forecast is «always cut low so that people can report overperformance later». The planner answers that nothing is being cut. One table settles it: put bias, the same ratio with the sign kept, next to the error.
tasks.goal: At the three month horizon and for each brand return brand, bias_pct (bias as a signed percentage of actuals) and wmape_pct (the error without its sign). Round both to one decimal. Sorted by bias_pct descending.
hints: Bias and error differ by one ABS: in the numerator of bias the sign survives, so shortfalls and overshoots cancel each other out, and here that is the point of the quantity rather than a defect.
The brand lives in the product reference table, so the forecast needs a second join, and the grouping runs on the brand.
tasks.explain: The director turned out to be right, though not about everyone: eight brands out of nine are forecast short by 5.9% to 14.7%, and that is exactly the systematic lean he described. The ninth breaks the picture. «Nettora» carries a bias of +11% together with the worst error on the list, 37.7%. The brand has been falling for two years while the planner keeps building in a return to the old level: the error there is not random, it all points one way. Hence how the two columns read. Error is about the quality of the model, bias is about the behaviour of the people who adjust it, and adjust it they always do: fear of a stockout pushes numbers up, a bonus for beating the plan pushes them down. Bias is also cheap to fix: a steady lean can be subtracted as a correction, and part of the error goes away without a single new model.

tasks.title: The forecast against the calendar
tasks.brief: Before arguing about how to improve the forecast, it is worth asking whether it beats the free alternative: «this month we will sell what we sold last month». That forecast needs no planner and no sign off meeting, only the previous row of actuals. The query works out the error of both on the same pairs.
tasks.goal: Predict how the comparison falls across the horizons.
tasks.predictQuestion: How will the two numbers fall across the three horizons?

options.label: One month ahead the forecast is twice as accurate as the calendar (15.4% against 33.3%), and at three months the difference nearly disappears: 30.9% against 33.5%
options.why: The forecast error grows with the horizon while the calendar error does not depend on the horizon at all: it looks only at the previous month of actuals and has no idea when it was «made». The two lines converge, and at the far horizon the forecast wins 2.6 points, less than a monthly cycle of sign off meetings costs.

options.label: The forecast wins by roughly a factor of two at all three horizons, because it uses more information
options.why: It has more information only at the near horizon. Three months before the start neither the retailer orders nor the promo plan are known, and the advantage over repeating last month nearly vanishes.

options.label: The calendar error grows with the horizon too, because it is worked out on the same pairs
options.why: The pairs are the same, but the calculation carries no horizon in it: a naive forecast for a month is the previous month of actuals, whatever lead time it was «announced» at. Small differences between horizons come only from the different sets of months.

options.label: The calendar will be more accurate at every horizon: repeating last month makes no assumptions
options.why: At the near horizon the forecast wins by more than a factor of two, and that is its legitimate value. It loses not everywhere but at the far horizon, where there was little left to lose.

hints: Ask about each line separately: what makes the forecast error move, and what makes the error of repeating last month move.
The forecast error at all three horizons is already worked out in sql-078: 15.4%, 27% and 30.9%.
tasks.explain: Comparing against a free benchmark is the first question to ask of any forecast, and here the answer is uncomfortable: one month ahead the forecast beats repeating last month twice over (15.4% against 33.3%), and at three months it wins 2.6 points (30.9% against 33.5%). The far horizon is exactly the one production and procurement need, the one where the forecast adds almost nothing to the calendar. The conclusion is not that the forecast is useless: at the near horizon it delivers exactly what it exists for. The conclusion is that the value of a forecast is measured by the distance to a benchmark rather than by its absolute error, and measured at each horizon separately. In practice this comparison is called forecast value added, and it is useful precisely because it turns «is our forecast good» into the checkable «is it better than nothing».

tasks.title: The forecast that takes value away
tasks.brief: sql-082 shows that at three months the forecast barely differs from repeating last month. The company average, however, says nothing about where it helps and where it gets in the way. The planner asks for the comparison broken down by brand: which ones to start the review with, and which to leave alone.
tasks.goal: Work out, for each brand at the three month horizon, the forecast error and the error of the «same as last month» benchmark, then say what to do with the table.

steps.goal: At the three month horizon and for each brand return brand, wmape_model (the forecast error), wmape_naive (the benchmark error) and gain_pp, the difference between them in percentage points, benchmark minus forecast. Round all three to one decimal. Sorted by gain_pp ascending.
hints: The benchmark is worked out before the join with the forecast: first actuals by month and SKU, then the previous month through a window function over the same SKU. Computed after the join, the window would see three rows per month, one per horizon, and shift by the wrong amount.
The first month of a series has no previous one, and LAG returns nothing there. Those pairs have to leave the comparison, otherwise the two errors are worked out on different sets of rows.

steps.question: For «Nettora» the forecast misses by 37.7% against 23.3% for the «same as last month» benchmark, while for «Pyrexan» it is 32.5% against 57.5%. What do you do with a table like this?
hints: Look at the sign of the difference rather than its size: it splits the brands into two different stories.
Ask which decision this table drives, and for which brands it changes anything at all.

options.label: Split the brands: where the difference is negative the forecast takes accuracy away, and until the cause is found the benchmark is the honest choice; on the rest it gives between five and twenty five points and needs nothing done to it
options.why: The table is not about the quality of the forecast in general but about where it works. A negative difference marks a brand where the planner manual work does worse than nothing, and there are two of those here. On «Pyrexan» and «Rhinolar» the same forecast wins 25 and 19 points, and there is no reason to touch it there.

options.label: Drop the forecast altogether: it is no better than repeating last month
options.why: That is how the company average reads, and only it. By brand the picture splits: on «Pyrexan» the forecast beats the benchmark by 25 points and on «Rhinolar» by 19. Dropping it would throw that part out along with the problem part.

options.label: Nothing: the difference for «Krosti» is 0.2 points, so the metric is unstable and it is too early to draw conclusions
options.why: One row near zero does not turn the other eight into noise. For «Nettora» the difference is 14.4 points and for «Pyrexan» it is 25; that is the forecast behaving differently on different brands, not a metric wobbling.

options.label: The benchmark wins on «Nettora» simply because the brand is falling: on a declining series repeating last month is more accurate by construction
options.why: On a declining series repeating last month overshoots too, since it always takes the higher previous level. It wins here only because the forecast overshoots harder: the bias on «Nettora» is +11% while every other brand sits below zero.

tasks.explain: The task brings two earlier findings together. The bias on «Nettora» was already visible in sql-081, where it looked like a quirk of one brand; the comparison with a benchmark shows what it costs: on that brand the forecast is 14.4 points worse than freely repeating last month. The opposite pole matters just as much. On «Pyrexan» the same forecast wins 25 points, so «the forecast is bad» is as wrong on this data as «the forecast is good». The right conclusion is addressed to somebody: review the brands with a negative difference rather than the method as a whole. Hence the working rule. Forecast accuracy on its own means nothing; what means something is the distance to a benchmark that costs nothing. And the caveat without which the rule lies: the benchmark here is the simplest one, «same as last month». For a seasonal product the fairer comparison is the same month a year ago, and this data allows that too, but whichever benchmark you pick has to be named out loud, because it sets the bar below which a forecast has no point.
